To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the proposed workload-aware index M(k) is never over-refine for irrelevant index or graph nodes, and that the proposed M(k)-index can be further improved in query performance by the M*(k) index, whose index nodes are organized in partition hierarchies.

we propose a novel multiresolution indexing scheme for XML that allows different parts of the graph to have different similarity requirements and that we propose a new index that is never over-refinied and that allows different parts to have different similarity requirement.
the M(k)-index provides a better index than D(k)-index and that the M*(k) index provides an even better index than the M(k)- index.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following problems: How to organize the index nodes so that the index size is small and the query performance is high, and how to take into account the workload information to improve the index quality.
the design and implementation of efficient structural indexes for path expression queries on semistructured databases.
the problem of how to index semistructured databases to speed up path expression query processing, and how to make the indexes more efficient in terms of index sizes and query processing times.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
M*(k)-Index is the best index in all aspects.
the proposed M(k)- and the M*(k) indexes are the best ones in terms of query answering performance, and that the M*(k)index is the best index in terms of query answer performance and index size.
our indexes provide a better solution for the problem of index size vs. query answering power trade-off.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our indexes can provide a more accurate trade-off between index space and query performance than previous indexes.
the workload-aware feature can improve the performance of path expression queries, but it is not always necessary to have the most refined partitions for the whole data graph.
we propose a family of indexes with different properties, and we provide a systematic study of how to choose an appropriate index to optimize the index size and the query performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a structural index should be aware of both workload and local similarity requirements.
the local similarity requirements for different parts of the index and the data graph can vary, and that the index structure should reflect this.
the local similarity requirement of an index node should be workload-aware, which can be achieved by a workload-aware index or a workload-aware index collection.
